review.diagram_merit: yes, as an optional finite example or indexing schematic
review.finding: A diagram or table can clarify how a permutation's reduced adjacent-transposition word lifts to a simple positive braid and why inversion number equals braid length. This would illustrate the algebraic statement; the proof itself is algebraic and does not need a crossing diagram.
review.map_direction: The lift is sigma ↦ hat(sigma), from S_n to the simple positive braids (the left/right divisors of Δ); π:B_n^+→S_n is the monoid homomorphism inverse to this lift on simple braids. A reduced expression s_i1...s_ik maps to the positive word σ_i1...σ_ik, and different reduced expressions yield the same braid by the cited reduced-word lift result.
review.composition_and_word_order: Use the source's homomorphism convention π(σ_i)=s_i, so π(σ_i1...σ_ik)=s_i1...s_ik. Make the permutation composition convention explicit in any example; do not reverse the factors when translating a displayed reduced word.
review.length_and_longest_element: For every τ, ℓ(hat(τ))=inv(τ). The longest element w0 has one-line notation (n,...,1), inversion number N=n(n−1)/2, and hat(w0)=Δ. For n=3, Δ=σ1σ2σ1=σ2σ1σ2; both are reduced expressions for w0.
review.divisibility_convention: A left divisor satisfies Δ=a c, so appears as a positive prefix; a right divisor satisfies Δ=c a, so appears as a suffix. The lemma proves the two divisor sets coincide, not that left and right divisibility orders coincide. Reversal exchanges the orders and sends the permutation label to its inverse.
review.diagram_specification: An optional n=3 example can list all six permutations with inversion counts and their simple lifts, grouped by reduced expressions, and highlight w0↔Δ. If showing crossings, label the generator sequence and avoid suggesting the schematic proves the all-n algebraic bijection. A compact map/table may communicate the general bijection more accurately than a single braid picture.
